text:
B: Alright, mate! Can you hear me?
A: Aye, yeah, hiya. I'm Craig.
B: Ryan. Stockport. Here, is that a Pools scarf on your door?
A: *(laughs)* Aye, Hartlepool. Didn't think anyone'd spot that.
B: Mate, I spot scarves. I've got County on the shelf here, look. Stockport County. Season ticket.
A: Oh, aye, I saw that on your photo. Yous were in the National League with us for a bit, weren't you?
B: We were, yeah, dark times. Dark times, Craig. Do you still go?
A: Er, when money allows, like. I had a season ticket for years. Me and me dad used to go every home game, from when I was about six. He's passed now, so it's sort of not the same. I watch most of 'em down the pub now, or on me phone.
B: Ah, sorry, mate. That's rough.
A: Nah, it's alright. It's a long time ago now. Still miss him at the football, mind.
B: Yeah. My dad had a heart scare a couple of years back, and it properly shook me, honestly. He's fine now, he's back moaning about the ref. But you think, don't you.
A: Aye. You do.
B: Anyway! What do you do for work, then?
A: Er, I'm a brickie. Well, I was. Done me back about eighteen month ago, so I'm off at the minute. Universal Credit and that. Bit embarrassing, to be honest.
B: Nah, don't be daft, that's not embarrassing. Backs go. Half my five-a-side lads have got a dodgy back and they still play, which is worse. What would you do instead, like, if you couldn't go back on the bricks?
A: I've been sort of thinking site supervisor, maybe. Or building maintenance. Something where I'm not lifting blocks all day. There's a course through the job centre I might look at.
B: You'd be good at that, you. You've got the calm face. Supervisors need the calm face. I haven't got it, my staff say I'm blunt. I am blunt, to be fair.
A: *(laughs)* Aye, I was always the one keeping the peace on site, like. Someone'd be kicking off about the weather and I'd just crack on.
B: See? That's a skill, that. I'm a manager, I run a bar in Manchester, and half the job's just stopping people kicking off. I'd hire you tomorrow.
A: Ha, I'd be no good behind a bar, I'd drop everything.
B: You'd be on the door, mate. Here, I'm going to be honest, I'm living in my sister's spare room at the minute. Since the divorce. Thirty-seven, in a single bed. So you're not the only one.
A: No way. I'm back at me mam's. Same bedroom I had when I was a kid. Divorce and all.
B: Ha! Look at us. The lads' club.
A: Aye. It's alright, though. Me mam does me tea, half five, mince and dumplings. Can't complain.
B: My sister does tea and all. Best thing about it. Do you have kids?
A: Me daughter, Ellie, she's nine. Every other weekend. That's her on the wall there.
B: Ah, she's got a cracking smile. Does she go to the match with you?
A: She's been once. She spent the whole game asking for chips.
B: That's the proper football experience, that. My nephew was the same, now he's correcting my stats in the car. Give it a couple of years, she'll be—
